t:
(a) Information on Usage.—Within 60 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Commandant of the Coast Guard shall—
        (1) determine the types and numbers of vessels typically transiting or utilizing that portion of the Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway beginning at a point that is due East of the outlet of the Cutler Drain Canal C–100 in Dade County, Florida, and ending at the Dade County line, during a period of 30 days; and 
        (2) provide the information on usage compiled under this subsection to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.  
    (b) Assessment of Certain Aids to Navigation.—Within 90 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Commandant of the Coast Guard shall—
        (1) review and assess the buoys, markers, and other aids to navigation in and along that portion of the Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway specified in subsection (a), to determine the adequacy and sufficiency of such aids, and the need to replace such aids, install additional aids, or both; and 
        (2) submit a report on the assessment required by this section to the committees.  
    (c) Submission of Plan.—Within 180 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Commandant shall submit a plan to the committees to address the needs identified under subsection (b).

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the required reports, assessment, and plan submission are a form of consultation. But every recipient is a congressional committee, and Congress is inside the federal government. The Coast Guard Commandant is not required to consult states, local governments, the public, or any other outside party, and no rulemaking, hearing, or right to sue is created.
fable.s: provide the information on usage compiled under this subsection to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure

qwen_block.w: This section requires the Commandant of the Coast Guard to submit reports and plans to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is an internal government action, not participation by outside parties. There is no requirement for consultation with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_block.s: provide the information on usage compiled under this subsection to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

opus.w: The section only requires the Coast Guard Commandant to collect usage data, assess navigation aids and send reports and a plan to congressional committees. Congress and its committees are inside the federal government, so this process never crosses the federal boundary. The tempting reading treats these reports and the plan as participation, but no outside party is consulted or given a say in any decision.
opus.s: provide the information on usage compiled under this subsection to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** The section requires the Coast Guard to study usage, assess navigation aids, and submit reports and a plan, which can look like formal process. But every recipient is a congressional committee, and Congress is inside the federal government. No state, local government, expert, company or member of the public is consulted, and there is no hearing, comment period, rulemaking or right to sue. So this does not count as participation.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Commandant of the Coast Guard to compile data and submit reports to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it constitutes internal government communication, not participation by outside parties. There is no requirement to consult with the public, states, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_chat.s: provide the information on usage compiled under this subsection to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Commandant must determine vessel usage and assess navigation aids, this involves interacting with the public or maritime industry. However, the text only requires the Commandant to *determine* and *provide* information to Congress. Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to it is not participation. There is no requirement to consult with the public, hold hearings, or coordinate with outside entities before making the determination or submitting the report.
